summary: Daily public transport ridership has rebounded to pre‑pandemic levels, while fuel savings remain substantial despite ultra‑low fuel prices. However, high mobility scores in retail, logistics and construction signal economic exposure and a risk of a modal shift toward private vehicles.

signals.detail: Weekly fuel savings of 35.7 million litres represent 42 % of the MCO peak, indicating continued behavioural change. The ultra‑low RM0.25/litre price, however, weakens price‑based incentives to sustain these savings.

Daily PT trips total 1.49 million, projecting roughly 545 million trips annually—slightly above the 2019 baseline of 522 million. The ridership component of the MF‑Index is at a perfect 100, confirming strong recovery.

Retail & Services, Logistics and Construction show mobility scores above 85 and are flagged HIGH risk, suggesting exposure to congestion, fuel price volatility and labor productivity losses. Their low WFH adoption (<15%) limits flexibility to mitigate these risks.

WFH adoption varies sharply: 60 % in Public & GLCs versus 5‑8 % in Logistics and Construction, creating unequal mobility burdens. Without targeted support, lower‑adoption sectors may face disproportionate cost pressures.

The MF‑Index at 54 signals a moderate shift away from private car use, yet the persistently low fuel price could erode this gain over time. Maintaining PT attractiveness and pricing signals will be key to locking in the current modal mix.

recommendation: Introduce a graduated fuel levy to raise RON95 to at least RM0.80/litre, earmarked for PT service upgrades and low‑emission vehicle incentives. Expand flexible WFH provisions for high‑risk sectors and launch a targeted subsidy for electric delivery fleets to curb future fuel demand.
